description: Somos un equipo enfocado en realizar innovación y herramientas para mejorar la vida de personas interesadas en la ciencia. Buscamos dar apoyo a todas las comunidades más vulnerables al proveerles conocimiento y mostrar que aún hay personas que se preocupan por ellas. Deseamos ser una fuente de cambio para el mundo para que cada generación pueda aspirar cada vez más alto.
summary:
Arrieros Mars Map is a hyperlocal field guide for the first astronauts to walk on Mars. Arrieros were the muleteers who opened trails across the Colombian Andes; Perseverance is our mule, and its tracks are the first trail in Jezero Crater.

The web app layers data from five NASA missions: HiRISE and CTX images and 1 m elevation, THEMIS night-time heat, Perseverance’s path and sample sites, Ingenuity’s flights and Curiosity’s weather. From them it plans the safest route plus a backup, avoiding steep and rough ground, and finds shelter spots at the foot of rock walls. The astronaut explores the ground in 3D, follows arrows and voice guidance, scans rocks to estimate minerals and flag toxic perchlorates, and gets alerts from MARTA, a simulated drone that spots dust storms and re-plans the route.

Every number shows how sure it is: measured by NASA, estimated from that data, or simulated for a future crewed mission.
details:
What it does
Arrieros Mars Map is a hyperlocal field guide for the first astronauts to walk on Mars. It covers two walking zones in Jezero Crater, the Delta front and Neretva Vallis. Existing tools like Mars Trek show the whole planet or a whole region. We zoom in to the few kilometers a person can actually cover on foot, and we combine the data so it answers the questions a crew will ask: Which way is safe? Where can I take cover? Do I have enough air to get back? What is this rock?

How it works

  • Map: HiRISE 25 cm orbital photos, with layers for slope, rough ground, night-time heat, relative radiation, shelters, Perseverance’s path, its sample sites and Ingenuity’s flights. Tap a sample site and the planner draws the safest route plus a backup route, with checkpoints every 150 m and a height profile.
  • Routes: We turn HiRISE (1 m) and CTX (20 m) elevation models into a cost grid. An A* search avoids slopes over 25° and very rough ground, and prefers the ground Perseverance already crossed, because it is proven passable.
  • Shelters: We look for flat, firm ground at the foot of rock walls. We measure how much sky the walls block with the elevation model, and use THEMIS night-time infrared to tell firm rock from loose sand.
  • Information access: Astronauts can access through the app to important details of the routes; as temperature, radiation, daylight left, fatigue and oxygen left. Moreover, they can reach this information by just speaking and using the microphone function in case they cannot open the app, it would tell them the results of their question instantly.
  • 3D: The same ground in 3D, from the astronaut’s eye level or flying along the route. This is used to simulate routes and look at all the probable thing that may happen.
  • Scan: The astronaut points a camera at a rock. The app measures colour, texture, layering, pits and veins from the pixels, estimates the rock type and likely minerals using Perseverance’s real findings nearby, and warns about toxic perchlorates in the dust. It then shows how a suit spectrometer would confirm the result. It can be used with phone camera, submitting images or choosing some samples provided.
  • Walk: Arrows over rover photos or the live phone camera, the phone compass, a step counter, and voice guidance in English and Spanish. A fatigue model simplifies the screen when the astronaut is exhausted. The audio used would be changed to the one of their relatives, to help their mental health. It guides you carefully through all the terrain.
  • MARTA: MARTA (Martian Aerial Real Time Data Assistance) is an integrated exploration and support system for human missions on Mars, consisting of a mobile rover and two autonomous hexacopters. The drones survey the terrain and collect aerial data, while the rover serves as a mobile base for transportation, data processing, storage, and recharging, providing astronauts with information to support safer decisions. This is used to recognize the terrain ahead, informing about hazards.
  • Earth twins: Each part of Jezero compared with similar places on Earth, such as Lake Salda, Atacama and Tatacoa in Colombia, using NASA satellite images. This is done by comparing data about some places in the world with their composition and rocks looking at which resembles more to the rcoks present and molecules present.

Benefits and intended impact
The app turns NASA data scattered across many missions into decisions a crew can make in seconds. That supports safety, NASA’s first priority, while leaving room for the science only humans can do on the spot. Today it is also a way to explore real Mars data for students and the public. The same method could plan safe routes for rescue teams or field expeditions on Earth.

How it is creative
The project is built around the story of the arrieros, the muleteers who opened trails across the Colombian Andes. Perseverance is our mule, and its tracks are the first trail on Mars. The app plays the real wind recorded by Perseverance’s microphone, links Martian rocks to Earth places that share their conditions, and introduces MARTA, a drone that watches the sky for the crew.

Factors we considered

  • Every number on screen is labelled Measured (NASA data), Estimated (calculated from NASA data) or Simulated (a concept for a future crewed mission), so the crew knows how much to trust it.
  • The design accounts for spacesuit mobility, Mars gravity (about 38% of Earth’s), fatigue, gloves and limited attention.
  • Mars has no GPS and no global magnetic field, so we explain how a crew could find its position instead.
  • Dust is the real storm hazard on Mars, not wind: it cuts visibility and solar power.
  • Messages to Earth arrive minutes late, so the crew must be able to decide on their own.
  • We considered about 40 problems that the astronauts could face and we chose the most importants. Here are all of them: How the system is recharged - Where the system is displayed - What time the routes are carried out - How to collect data in real time - What to do if a spacesuit fails - How to create a system that keeps the astronaut warm - Which area will be explored and why (the goal), including finding interesting places to explore - What season we land in and where - How to make the most of the resources at hand - How to protect everything during a storm - Which minerals can be brought back and whether they need to be disinfected - How to coexist with meteorites - How to use already-tested vehicles to explore better - How we imagine the base of our project - Microgravity - Radiation - Resources and conditions needed to survive - Communication - Safe ground to walk on, including soil that may be toxic or impossible to step on - Recognizing weather conditions such as storms, including changes that existing systems may fail to detect - Knowing escape routes - Orientation and knowing where you are - Tool materials - An efficient route that saves time and fuel - Thermal conditions - Concise, easy-to-access information - Not understanding landmarks - Telling what is interesting apart from what is dangerous - The helmet visor fogging up - Parts of the spacesuit wearing out - Carbon dioxide having nowhere to escape - Preparing and eating food - Confinement or monotony affecting the astronauts’ health - Samples mixing or getting contaminated - Difficulty running biology experiments because of limited space or labs - An element changing its composition when moved to another planet - Air leaking through the joints of the base - Difficulty treating health problems - No spare parts available if something breaks - Problems with water recycling

Tools
HTML, CSS and JavaScript; Leaflet, three.js, Lucide icons, driver.js and TensorFlow.js with COCO-SSD; Python and Node.js with geotiff.js for data processing; the Web Speech API for voice; Git and Vercel for hosting; FFmpeg and Puppeteer for the video. We built and tested it on a laptop and on phones, using their camera, compass and step counter; Anthropic (claude).
